title: Harriet Tubman Goes Back for Her Family
text:
Harriet Tubman escaped from slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland, in 1849, walking north to Philadelphia. She later said that when she crossed into freedom she felt like she was in heaven, but she was a stranger in a strange land, because her family was still in slavery. She decided to bring them out.

In 1850 she helped her niece and the niece's two children escape after they had been put up for sale. In 1851 she returned for her husband, John, only to find he had married another woman and would not come. She brought out others instead.

At Christmas 1854 she came back for three of her brothers, who were about to be sold. They hid near their parents' cabin. According to her biographer Sarah Bradford, their father brought them food but kept his eyes covered, so that if he were questioned, he could truthfully say he had not seen them. Their mother was not told, because it was feared she would cry out.

In 1857, learning that her father was in danger of arrest for helping fugitives, Tubman returned for her aged parents. Unable to walk far, they rode in a makeshift cart she arranged. She took them all the way to St. Catharines, in Canada. The abolitionist William Still, who kept records of fugitives passing through Philadelphia, noted several of these escapes. In all, Tubman made about thirteen trips and freed some seventy people, many of them her own relatives.
lesson: Personal freedom can feel incomplete while those we love remain in danger. Going back for others is the truest test of what we have gained.
people: Harriet Tubman, Ben and Rit Ross, her brothers
location: Dorchester County, Maryland, USA, and St. Catharines, Ontario, Canada
source: Sarah Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869); William Still, The Underground Railroad (1872); Kate Clifford Larson, Bound for the Promised Land (2004)
